sentences.text: Bergisuchus is an extinct genus of mesoeucrocodylian belonging to the sebecosuchian group, and it was a small terrestrial hypercarnivore.
This animal possessed a snout shape quite different from the broad, flat snouts of modern crocodilians, featuring a tall, laterally compressed snout with tall nasals forming a raised, sharp midline.

Bergisuchus had relatively narrow, serrated teeth similar to predatory theropod dinosaurs, unlike the conical teeth of modern crocodilians, and its large lower canine tooth was approximately 2 cm tall.
Huge, exaggerated canines in Bergisuchus may have functioned as sexual signals or weapons in intraspecific competition rather than for predation.
Bergisuchus was first discovered in 1966 by Dr. Dietrich Berg in the Messel Pit, Germany, and the genus was established by him that same year.

The genus was formally named and described in 1968 by the German paleontologist Oskar Kuhn, who named the species Bergisuchus dietrichbergi to honor Dr. Berg and used the Greek suffix suchos meaning 'crocodile'.
The holotype specimen, a snout and lower jaw, was found in the Messel Pit near Darmstadt and reported in 1966, while another jaw was found in an open-pit coal mine near Halle in Saxony-Anhalt.
An additional incomplete pair of lower jaws was found in the Geiseltal coal mine near Halle, Saxony-Anhalt.
Bergisuchus was originally classified as a sebecosuchian, supposedly the first found outside South America, and later assigned to Trematochampsidae in 1988.
Researchers suggest Bergisuchus was likely a fast, terrestrial predator rather than an aquatic ambush hunter.
Researchers suggest the front-heavy teeth of Bergisuchus were a specialization for hunting large prey by delivering powerful bites at the jaw's front.
Researchers suggest Bergisuchus used large front canines as fangs and smaller rear teeth to chew food before swallowing.

In 2000, Rossmann and colleagues assigned Bergisuchus to its own monotypic family, the Bergisuchidae, based on its distinctness from Sebecus, and the family Bergisuchidae was established by Rossmann et al. in 2000 as the only representative.
Bergisuchus lived during the Early to Middle Eocene epoch, with fossils found at the Messel fossil site in Germany dating to the Lutetian stage, between 48.07 and 41.03 million years ago.

Bergisuchus is known primarily from the Eocene Messel Pit in Germany, and it indicates that sebecosuchians were once more widespread in Europe than later in the Cenozoic, when they were restricted to South America.

While phylogenetic analyses support Bergisuchus as a close relative of Sebecus, the exact interrelationships between Bergisuchus, Sebecidae, and other clades remain unsettled, as different phylogenetic analyses have produced conflicting results, with some excluding Bergisuchus from Sebecidae and others placing it well within the family.

The presence of Bergisuchus in Europe is regarded as evidence for a connection between South American and European faunas in the early Eocene, though this is debated, and it is suggested that Bergisuchus descended from a separate invasion from South America during the Palaeogene rather than from Cretaceous European sebecosuchians like Doratodon.
